#5500. The 2026 Manhattan Wealth Rush: Ultraluxury Real Estate Is Smashing Sales Records

The Manhattan luxury market has had a banner year despite the pied-à-terre tax and the recent stock market correction.

Trophy properties—those priced $10 million and above—made up half the contracts signed last week, leading the luxury market into the second biggest year in two decades, according to Olshan Realty.

As of Nov. 22, an impressive 294 contracts were signed at $10 million and above, not far off the peak year of 2021, when 400 were signed. The average asking price for last week was $10.5 million, and properties were moving with a fairly low 5% average discount.

Corcoran's Deborah Grubman, who co-listed last week's most expensive sale—a $28.75 million triplex in the Pritzker Prize–winning Richard Meier building in the West Village—says that the luxury market normally shows signs of slowing down around the Thanksgiving holiday. But not this year.

"New York is still a very desirable destination for people of wealth," she tells Realtor.com®.

The glass triplex at 176 Perry St.—one of the city's most coveted blocks—was owned by Broadway and movie star Hugh Jackman. The condo, built in 2001, had been on and off the market since June 2022, and at one point was priced at $39 million.

Jackman and his ex-wife, Deborra-Lee Furness, purchased the 11,000-square-foot minimalist abode for $21 million in 2008. Spanning the eighth, ninth and 10th floors, it is "one of the most dramatic apartments in Manhattan," the listing states.

The full-service condominium comes with sweeping views of the river and Hudson River Park and is within walking distance of The High Line, Little Island, the Meatpacking District, Bleecker Steet, and the Whitney Museum. Jean-Georges Vongerichten's Perry Street Restaurant is on its ground floor.

The Richard Meier building, one of the first ultraluxe buildings that far west, helped change the face of the once-gritty area.

"It was the first 'star-chitect' building in the West Village on the waterfront," says the broker. "It was groundbreaking in terms of luxury. At the time, people said, 'Who is going to live in the highway?' It predated all that green space."

While it took Jackman about five years to unload the property, Grubman says that the West Village—and Perry Street, which stretches from Greenwich Avenue to the river—remains in high demand.

"It's a street that's got lots of charm and history," she says. "The West Village is out of central casting. You still have the charm of the small townhouses and tree-lined streets.

"The only thing that's really changed a lot is the price point."

Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman represented the buyer of one of the year's top sales: a $16.5 million, 3,855-square-foot condo in the Waldorf Astoria Residences at 301 Park Ave. in Midtown.

The luxury broker says her trophy property sales for 2026 are on track to beat her previous best year, which was 2021.

That year, when 400 ultraluxe contracts were signed, those who weren't fleeing lockdowns were shelling out for multimillion-dollar properties, spurred on by historically low interest rates in the 2% to 4% range.

Today, with higher rates hovering around 7%, there are plenty of cash-flush buyers snapping up ultraluxe homes. (Some still prefer 7% mortgage rates to pulling their money out of more lucrative investments.)

"The phrase that sums up 2026 for me is 'bidding wars,'" the broker tells Realtor.com. "This year will go down as my best year."

She attributes the surging high-end market to a couple of factors: tight inventory pushing up prices and sparking intense competition, and the "insanely high and insanely competitive" rental market, with rents double or triple what they were just a few years ago.

According to Realtor.com, a three-bedroom-plus in Manhattan has a median monthly rent of $5,375, an increase of 35.6% over the past seven years, requiring a household to earn $215,000 a year just to stay afloat with rent.

However, those who want a luxury three-bedroom-plus abode in a trendy neighborhood can shell out significantly more. Griffith says that a few years ago, a large luxury dwelling in an area like Tribeca could cost around $19,000 a month. But now?

"It would work itself up close to $30,000," she says. "So those people are saying, 'Do I want to spend $30,000 a month or should I pivot and think about buying something? How much am I going to overspend before I say, 'OK, let me buy'?"

Combine stratospheric rents with "inventory levels down across the board," and prices have skyrocketed.

"If you have something good in the West Village, in Tribeca, on the Upper East Side, it is likely going to trade itself up in a bidding war," says the agent.

When dream turnkey apartments began to disappear from listings, buyers became more willing to take on projects, resulting in a stronger-than-normal luxury co-op market. In general, co-ops are much older—and cheaper—than condos.

While the week ending Nov. 22 saw luxury condos outpace co-ops 18-4, there have been several weeks during 2026 when that gap was considerably narrower—and one week in June when co-ops won out.

"These are places that might require several million dollars to renovate," says Griffith. "And now that market too is getting absorbed."

She says those who didn't leave the city during the COVID-19 pandemic—fleeing to Westchester, Connecticut, or Florida—are the die-hards who are committed to the city long term. And they are the ones out there bidding up and buying.

Especially relevant are families whose children are deep in the school system.

"They're putting down roots for a minimum of 10 to 15 years," she says.

Despite her banner year, Griffith says she isn't planning a celebration just yet. Next year could be a different story as the pied-à-terre surcharge ramps up to replace Department of Finance valuations with significantly higher "fair market" valuations for 2029.

"This year was an emotional journey," she says. "There were many bidding wars we won, but also many we lost. I'm the type who focuses more on, 'What are the deals that we lost?'"

The second-highest contract of the week was a $25 million sponsor duplex penthouse at 133 E. 73rd St. Listing agency Modlin Group did not return a request for more information.

#5499. Planning To Sell in 2027? Start Prepping Now.

If selling your house is on your calendar for 2027, you may be thinking you’ve got plenty of time. Maybe you’re aiming for January. Maybe you’re waiting for spring. Either way, next year probably feels far enough away that getting ready can wait, too.

But waiting until 2027 to sell doesn’t mean waiting until 2027 to get started.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from than they’ve had in years. So, if you want your house to stand out when it’s time to list, a little preparation now can make a big difference later.

As a general rule of thumb, Zillow recommends giving yourself about 2-3 months to get your house ready to list. And that makes sense when you consider that the vast majority of sellers (78%) did at least one home improvement project before their house hit the market.

That gives you plenty of time to decide what to fix, find contractors, get on their schedules, actually make the updates, and get everything ready for photos and showings.

But don’t worry – that doesn’t mean every seller had some big to-do. The most common? Interior painting (see graph below):

That certainly doesn’t mean you need to tackle everything on this list. You may not need to do any of it. But odds are there’s at least one project you’ll want to do. And starting that conversation now gives you a leg up before next year.

While you might have a long list of things you think need updating, that doesn’t mean they’re all worth the time, effort, or money.

An agent will help you figure out which projects deserve a spot on your to-do list based on what buyers want most and what other sellers are doing. That way, you’re not investing in updates that won’t make much of a difference when you sell.

One thing your agent may recommend today is that you go ahead and get a pre-listing inspection. It’s basically your cheatsheet to what a buyer’s inspection may turn up later on.

And now that buyers have more options, they’re pickier – and you don’t want anything popping up in an inspection that could put them off.

For example, you know that HVAC system you’ve been hoping will make it through one more season? Now’s a good time to give it some attention – along with anything else you know needs a little TLC. That way a repair you could’ve handled months ago won’t become a surprise in the middle of your sale.

According to Angi, a pre-listing inspection typically costs $300-600 and that can be money well spent. As the National Association of Realtors (NAR) explains:

“An inspector will be able to give you a good indication of the trouble areas that will stand out to potential buyers, and you’ll be able to make repairs before open houses begin.”

The advantage isn’t just knowing what may come up, but being able to get ahead of it and space out the projects on your own schedule. So you don’t feel stressed during go-time.

But remember, not everything needs to happen right away. Some things are better saved for when you’re closer to listing.

Think deep cleaning, staging, touching up paint, and tidying up the landscaping. Those are the finishing touches that’ll help your house look its best when buyers walk through the door.

But there’s one thing you can start anytime: decluttering. Go ahead and tackle the closets, garage, or storage room you’ve been avoiding. Future you will appreciate having a few less boxes to pack.

The idea isn’t to get everything done today. It’s to spread the work out so you’re not scrambling when listing day arrives. As Redfin puts it:

“Smart preparation leads to a smoother sale, stronger offers, and fewer surprises during closing. . . Homes that are clean, well-staged, priced right, and professionally photographed tend to sell quickly.”

You don't need to spend the rest of the year renovating your house or packing up your life. But you can start making a plan.The earlier you figure out what needs to be done, the more time you'll have to do it right. #5498. Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief

A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer-class GPUs without pushing them into lock-in or loose data handling.

In Stuttgart, the HammerHAI AI factory is taking shape around a system from Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. using Nvidia Corp. Grace Blackwell chips. The center’s pitch leans as much on people as on processors, according to Bastian Koller (pictured), managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart.

“It’s very important to bring them there because everybody’s talking about AI, but we focus especially on SMEs and startups,” Koller said. “So some startups know what they want, some startups want to try and they need help and support.”

Koller spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how HammerHAI avoids lock-in, its pragmatic approach to sovereignty and a concierge model that pairs each customer with a consistent contact. (* Disclosure below.)

Industrial users no longer want shell programming; they expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The center has already worked with customers on existing systems while it waits on the new hardware, and several have produced success stories. Rather than holding onto them, it designs its services so workloads can leave, according to Koller.

“The idea is to evolve the system and the services in a way that they can simply move from us to a hyperscaler or from hyperscaler back,” Koller said. “Because what we are doing is, we give them a boost, we push them forward.”

That pragmatism extends to sovereignty itself. The Stuttgart center runs an ISO-certified environment with TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work. Full independence, down to European chips, is not realistic in the near term, Koller explained.

“We cannot now say, okay, come back in 10 years when we have a sovereign processor or a sovereign GPU or something like this,” Koller said. “We have to look for the data.”

Efficiency is part of the equation, too. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. The bigger lesson is human: A concierge model pairs each customer with a consistent contact, according to Koller.

“We learn more how the users are working and thinking, to be honest,” Koller said. “… We can build up a system which is highly fancy, whatever there, nobody will use it because we never thought about what the user needs.”

#5497. Bitcoin and Ethereum Bounce Back: Market Finally Turning?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin and Ethereum are bouncing back after a brutal selloff, but the recovery is running into a market that still looks far from healthy. Bitcoin climbed back above $60,000 over the weekend after touching a low near $55,250. Ethereum also gained ground, its first breath of air after several days of relentless selling, a good day for crypto despite bad news and uncertainty.

U.S. stocks suffered another heavy selloff on Friday, with the Nasdaq losing more than 5% as people questioned AI valuations and spending. Asian markets followed lower today, while Bitcoin recovered. Crypto buyers are stepping in, though it doesn’t yet signal that risk appetite has returned.

Crypto will face a tougher test as traditional markets reopen. We are watching technology stocks, oil prices, Treasury yields, and Federal Reserve expectations for clues. A lasting turnaround would need more than short-covering and bargain hunting. It needs buyers willing to hold positions while uncertainty remains high.

The bounce followed a sharp liquidation wave that dragged Bitcoin toward $55,000, its lowest level since September 2024. Yet, this kind of flush can create room for a rebound. Forced sellers disappear, short positions begin closing, and investors who waited on the sidelines see more attractive entry prices.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are still recording outflows, including a $582 million withdrawal at the end of the week. BlackRock’s IBIT alone suffered $541 million in outflows during the session.

Technically, Bitcoin needs to turn $60,000 into support rather than another rejection. Holding above that psychological level would improve its short-term structure. A move toward $62,000 would give bulls a more meaningful foothold, while a drop toward the recent low would put the recovery in jeopardy.

Ethereum faces a similar challenge, but its performance against Bitcoin matters just as much as its dollar price. If ETH begins outperforming BTC, it could signal that traders are becoming comfortable taking on additional risk. If Bitcoin leads while Ethereum remains weak, the market may still be hiding in the safest corner of crypto even if we see news and catalysts from geopolitics.

The bigger threat to the recovery may come from outside the crypto market. Friday’s selloff hammered technology stocks, sending the Nasdaq down 5.3% and pushing the S&P 500 into correction territory. Investors are questioning AI spending and if it can justify enormous valuations, creating pressure across risk assets.

Bitcoin has increasingly behaved like a high-beta technology trade during periods of stress. When people reduce exposure to growth stocks, crypto gets caught in the same wave. A stabilization in Nasdaq trading could provide an important tailwind, especially if investors begin buying beaten-down technology shares again.

Oil offers another important signal as Brent crude hovers around $92 a barrel, and WTI trades at $83. Both benchmarks had fallen during the previous week, and lower oil prices could help ease inflation pressure, potentially giving the Federal Reserve more flexibility and reducing pressure on bond yields. That would improve conditions for assets sensitive to liquidity.

BREAKING: US stock market futures rebound as markets reopen for the first time since the Nasdaq 100's worst week since 2020:1. S&P 500: +1.4%2. Nasdaq 100: +2.2%3. Dow Jones: +0.9%4. WTI Crude: +1.5%5. Gold: +2.0%S&P 500 futures are back above 7000.

Gold also rebounds after suffering its steepest weekly decline since March. Bullion rose as traders reassessed interest-rate expectations, but its recovery remains fragile. If gold, stocks, and crypto begin stabilizing together, combined with good geopolitical news, it would suggest forced selling is easing across markets. If equities continue falling, temporary rebounds might disappear quickly.

Today, Bitcoin and Ethereum are showing signs of life, not confirmation of a new trend. Bitcoin needs to hold its reclaimed levels, ETF demand must improve, and Wall Street needs to stop bleeding. Until those pieces fall into place, this bounce may be the market catching its breath rather than preparing for another rally.

#5496. A Fixer-Upper Could Be Your Path To Homeownership

When the homes you love keep landing outside your budget, it may be time to look at the ones other buyers skip.

A fixer-upper won’t be the right call for everyone. Plenty of buyers want a home that’s ready on move-in day. But homes that need some updating could get you in the door for a lot less.

More buyers are starting to realize it too. And Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, explains why:

“Fixer-uppers give buyers a way to break into the housing market at a time when affordability is still stretched thin. For those with the vision. . . fixer-uppers provide both a starting point in the market and the chance to create a home that’s truly their own.”

If that sounds like you, here’s why a fixer-upper could be worth a closer look.

Because these homes need work, they tend to have a lower asking price up front. According to AmeriSave, fixer-uppers usually sell for 20% to 30% less than what they’re worth on the market.

Here’s what that could look like. KCM applied a 25% discount – the middle of that range – to the median home price from the National Association of Realtors (NAR). This is an example, not the average price of a fixer-upper. But it shows the savings could top $100,000 (see graph below):

That’s a big difference up front and it could be what gets you into a home today. And odds are you don’t have to tackle all the repairs at once – you can space them out over time as it works for you.

Just remember repair costs can add up quickly and eat into those savings if you don’t plan ahead. So, before you make an offer, get estimates from a contractor and set a repair budget you’re comfortable with. There are even some loan types designed to help pay for the work.

With a renovation loan, you can roll the cost of the work into your mortgage, so you don’t have to cover it all out of pocket once you move in. Here are a few options from FHA, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the VA (see visual below):

Each program has its own rules, and not every lender offers all of them. So, talk to a trusted lender to see which options are available to you and which make sense for how you plan to tackle updates and repairs over time.

Some cities even offer tax breaks to buyers who renovate a fixer-upper and raise its value. These programs vary by location, so check with your city or a tax professional to see what’s available where you want to live.

If you want to check for more information yourself, go to your local county or city official dot-gov website. Then, use the search bar and look for: [City or County Name] AND “home rehabilitation” OR “property tax incentive” OR “housing repair”

A local agent can also help you find fixer-uppers in the neighborhoods you have your heart set on.

If move-in-ready homes keep coming in over budget, a home that needs some TLC could be your way in. #5495. Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith’s $42 Million Calabasas Home Erupts in Flames

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's $42 million Los Angeles property went up in flames after their shed caught fire.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station responded to a 911 call at the property in the early hours of Nov. 23.

Officials told People that they arrived to discover a "structure fire" at the couple's Calabasas home. They added that no one was hurt.

“It appears a shed caught fire, and the cause is believed to be accidental,” the statement from the sheriff's department revealed.

In audio from the 911 call obtained from Page Six, firefighters can be heard saying, "We do have a shed on fire with no spread to the brush."

An emergency personnel noted that they were already "on scene," and then another firefighter explained that the fire had been "downgraded to a structure."

The couple's Calabasas property serves as their primary residence. Set on 150 acres, the estate—which they began working on in 1997, the same year they tied the knot—features high-end amenities, including a basketball court, a tennis court, and a massive swimming pool.

The property was designed by architect Stephen Samuelson, who teamed up with Smith and Pinkett Smith in 1997, after they were inspired by the work he had done on the home of Carol Burnett, according to Architectural Digest.

However, it was to be a labor of love for the couple—who had to wait four years to secure the permits to begin construction on their dream home. It would sit at the center of an enormous property that they had amassed over time by buying up adjacent plots of land as they became available.

In the end, Smith and Pinkett Smith created an idyllic Mediterranean-inspired sanctuary for their family, boasting all manner of luxury from a meditation lounge and a recording studio to a sunken trampoline.

It was previously believed that Smith and Pinkett Smith were living apart, with the actress revealing during a previous "Today" interview that she had moved into a new abode in the Los Angeles area. She did not reveal any other details about the property.

The fire comes after Smith, 58, and Pinkett Smith, 55, were spotted in a rare outing alongside their children, Jaden, 28, and Willow, 26.

Last year, the couple put one of their many homes on the market for the relatively low price of $2 million—amid rampant speculation over the state of their marriage.

Many fans have been questioning the status of their relationship since 2022, when Smith infamously slapped Chris Rock across the face during the Oscars ceremony after the comedian made a joke about Pinkett Smith's hair.

Then, just over a year later, Pinkett Smith sensationally revealed during an interview on the "Today" show that she and Smith had been living "completely separate lives" since 2016, despite insisting that they had no plans to legally divorce.

In the two years since that candid confession, questions have continued to be swirl about the truth of their relationship, with Smith sending the rumor mill into overdrive again in February when he put on a very raunchy display with singer India Martínez during an on-stage performance of their song, "First Love."

Following that public display, the "Men In Black" actor pushed forward a new album, titled "Based on a True Story," marking the first time he has launched a new record in years.

According to Smith, the album is the result of "self-examination" that began after the Oscars incident, which saw the actor banned from all academy events for 10 years.

"I’ve taken the last couple of years to really do a deep dive on the parts of me that may or may not been in that level of certainty and asking those deep scary internal questions," he told the Associated Press.

"It really is the result of my initial self-examination. Every song is about some part of myself that I discovered or wanted to explore, something I wanted to share. It’s the most full musical offering that I’ve ever created."

#5494. 3 Housing Questions That Might Come Up at Your Next Family Dinner

This time of year usually means more time spent with family and friends. And in recent years, when everyone gets together, the conversation has a way of drifting to housing.

Your uncle is sure home prices are about to crash. Your cousin heard foreclosures are surging. And someone across the table brings up the word “recession.”

If you’ve wondered about any of this yourself, that makes sense. There’s a lot of noise out there. So let’s look at what the data actually shows, so you’ll have real answers the next time it comes up.

Let’s start with your uncle’s crash prediction. The short answer is no. Experts project home prices will keep climbing nationally in 2027.

On average, forecasters expect prices to rise about 1.4% next year (see graph below). That’s slower than the big jumps of a few years ago, but it’s still growth, not a crash.

Prices are dipping in some markets, though. It just depends on where you live. Lawrence Yun, Chief Economist at the National Association of Realtors (NAR), explains why:

“Price declines are occurring mainly in southern states, where there has been robust new home construction in recent years. Given the region’s faster job growth, these price drops should be viewed as temporary and as a second-chance opportunity for those previously priced out of the market.”

So, the dips that are fueling all the social media chatter are limited to select areas, and experts think they’ll be short-lived. It doesn’t mean a crash is looming.

If you’re thinking about moving, look at the numbers for your area.

Then your cousin chimes in about foreclosures. They’ve ticked up lately, but here’s some important context. That’s compared to very low levels. They’re still below where they were before the pandemic, according to ATTOM.

So, why doesn’t today look like 2008? Logan Mohtashami, Lead Analyst at HousingWire, explains:

“. . . we have had many recessions post-WWII but only one foreclosure crisis. That foreclosure crisis started with a massive credit boom from 2002-2005, and then a credit bust. . . none of that is happening now . . .“

Today’s homeowners also have something a lot of people didn’t have back then – equity. In every state, the average homeowner with a mortgage has more than $100,000 of it, according to Cotality (see map below):

If a homeowner hits a rough patch, they can usually sell their house instead of facing foreclosure.

While someone in your family may be convinced a recession is coming, experts don’t agree. The average forecast from The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists puts the odds at about 24%, so most experts aren’t expecting one. And that’s a good thing.

But even if one hits, history shows a recession doesn’t mean home prices will automatically fall. In 5 of the last 6 recessions, prices actually went up, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) (see graph below):

The one exception was 2008, the only one of these recessions that started in the housing market itself.

So, the next time your uncle predicts a crash or your cousin brings up 2008, you’ll know prices aren’t crashing, foreclosures are still low, and a recession doesn’t automatically spell trouble for housing. If a move in 2027 is on your mind, connect with a local real estate agent to look at what prices are doing in your neighborhood so you can plan with real local numbers, not scary headlines.

#5493. Robotics component maker coprod raises $6M to take on robotics ‘integration hell’

Robotics component maker coprod Inc. announced today that it has raised $6 million in new funding to reduce the time and costs associated with building new robotic platforms.

The funding is intended to enable the company to bring its first line of components to market. Founded in 2024, coprod offers an ecosystem of compatible hardware components for robotics and physical artificial intelligence applications.

It works alongside a software application programming interface and a front-end configuration tool to interconnect the components and standardize the communication between them, while preserving the real-time performance required for safe and reliable hardware.

At the core of coprod’s offering is the co:system, which combines the company’s modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane with one API in C++ and Python. The product family includes co:power, co:battery, co:sensor and co:motion, with each module able to be used as part of a complete system or integrated on its own.

Coprod is tackling the issue wherein most component suppliers support many protocols in the hope of catering to any integrator, which means their parts rarely work together out of the box. The result, according to coprod, is that building a system from mix-and-match components puts a heavy burden on the integrator. It requires two to three years of custom electronics and software work common before a system is reliable, in a phase known in the industry as “integration hell.”

The company claims that with its stack, the same work requires only a small team of roboticists, $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration and a few months of time.

“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Loïc Delineau.

Coming into its new funding round, coprod’s components are already powering multiple robots in Switzerland, including the ETH Robotics Club’s XALUN, the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, which took its first steps in Zurich in recent weeks. The company is also establishing partnerships with robotics integrators and well-known labs to validate its first hardware prototypes before launching them on the market early next year.

The funding is also intended to support a new hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is expected to cut the company’s development cycles from two weeks to 24 hours. Testing at the site will be used to produce datasheets and digital twin models for each component, an effort aimed at narrowing the gap between simulated and real-world performance that arises in robotics development.

By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line on the market, qualified and certified. Large-scale production is planned for both Shenzhen and Texas, with the company’s headquarters and research and development remaining in Switzerland.

Component supply has also emerged as a constraint for robot makers, particularly in humanoids. A McKinsey & Co. analysis published in April found that supply chain bottlenecks for humanoids are most likely to emerge around actuators and sensing and perception systems, the type of hardware coprod is developing.

Delineau formed coprod with Chief Technology Officer Vincent Nguyen and Chief Scientist Matthias Schuller (pictured), all graduates of the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne. The three started out by building a bipedal robot demonstrator in a parent’s garage in the Swiss Alps to show what compatible components could do.

Founderful AG and Prototype Capital led the pre-seed round, with General Catalyst Group Management, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital and Venture Kick also participating. Angel investors in the round include Hugging Face Inc. co-founder Thomas Wolf, the Dassault family and Florent Perrichon. Venture Kick awarded coprod CHF 40,000 ($47,600) earlier this year.

Andreas Klinger, founder of Prototype, said coprod is fixing “the biggest problem in hardware.” It argues that robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware so they can focus on the parts of their products that create value for customers.

#5492. 3 Things Sellers Need To Know About Pricing Today

If you’re getting ready to sell your house, you’ve probably heard how important it is to price it right. And that’s especially true right now.

Today’s buyers have more homes to choose from and they’re feeling pinched by today’s mortgage rates. That makes them more selective. And that means having the right pricing strategy matters more than ever.

That starts with understanding these three things. Because, with the right approach, you can still put your house in a great position to sell.

It’s natural to look at what your neighbor’s house sold for and think yours should sell for something similar. And those comparable sales (or comps) absolutely matter. But they only tell part of the story. Here’s why.

Buyers aren’t shopping against what sold three or even six months ago. They’re comparing your house to what’s available right now.

That’s why your agent will look at more than just recent sales. They’ll also consider the houses currently for sale, what’s going under contract, and how your house stacks up against those options to find the right price for your house.

The goal isn’t necessarily to price lower than everyone else. It’s to make sure buyers see the value in choosing your house over the competition.

As Jake Krimmel, Senior Economist at Realtor.com explains:

“Pricing to today’s demand is helping homes move and keeping more transactions alive in a high-rate environment.”

Understanding how your house compares to what’s available today can help you feel more confident in your asking price.

Getting your asking price right puts you in a stronger position from the start. But when an offer comes in, remember that price is only one part of the equation.

Today’s buyers may still negotiate on things like money toward closing costs or repairs, even when a house is priced well – and that’s not necessarily a commentary on your price, it’s just the norm for negotiation in today’s market.

According to Redfin, 44.7% of home sales involve seller concessions. That’s just under half. And 15.8% had both a price reduction and a concession.

Now, that doesn’t mean you have to agree to everything a buyer asks for. But sometimes offering a closing-cost credit or helping with a mortgage rate buydown could be what seals the deal. Other times, holding firm is the better move. Your agent will help you decide.

The best advice? Look at the whole offer, including what you’ll actually walk away with, to decide what’s right for you.

Even with a competitive price, some houses take longer to sell than others. And if yours isn’t getting the attention or offers you expected, that doesn’t mean your sale is off track. It just means it’s time to take a closer look at what’s happening.

Your agent can help you use buyer feedback and local market activity to figure out what adjustments, if any, could make a difference.

Are buyers seeing your listing online but not scheduling showings? Maybe the photos or presentation aren’t doing your house justice.

Are people touring but not making offers? It could be the condition, the price, or how your house compares to others they’ve seen.

And if buyers are making offers, but the terms aren’t working for you, that may call for a different negotiation strategy altogether.

While you may worry that means you have to drop your price, that’s not always true. A price cut can help, but only if it addresses what’s keeping buyers from making a move.

That’s why feedback, local competition, and an agent who knows how to interpret both are so important.

Selling successfully today isn't about finding one magic number and hoping everything falls into place. #5491. Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter

An uninsulated garage might seem like no big deal, but come the winter months, it can do more harm than good.

In fact, when a garage lacks proper insulation during the colder months, frozen pipes, heat loss, and damaged items are bound to arise.

Fortunately, insulation solutions and preventive measures can help you avoid these issues while protecting your garage, your car, and your home.

An uninsulated garage in the winter months can cause a chain reaction of issues to the home itself. One of the most common risks is frozen pipes.

“When the plumbing or water lines located in the garage get exposed to below-freezing temps, they may freeze and cause water damage,” explains Chris Boyle, in-house repair tech at Parts Town Home and Fix.com in Nova Scotia.

Additionally, improperly insulated garages can prompt heat loss throughout the entire home.

“Many poorly insulated garages share foundations with homes. As a result, cold air may circulate through the living spaces and force families to turn up their heating systems,” says Boyle.

Not only does this put a strain on HVAC systems, it can also drive up monthly heating bills.

Plus, poor insulation may damage items stored in the garage, particularly car batteries, which can lose charge or fail completely.

So, how do you know for sure whether your garage is insulated?

On a cold day, compare the temperature inside your garage to the outside.

If your garage feels as cold as the outdoors, or if the rooms adjacent to it are always noticeably colder in the winter, there’s a good chance it’s not insulated.

“You can also inspect the walls and ceiling for visible insulation. On the garage door, thin or hollow panels usually indicate a lack of insulation, while thicker panels often mean insulating material is present,” explains Paul Sharpe, owner at Surfside Garage Doors in Toms River, NJ.

Once you determine you have an uninsulated garage, here are several tips to keep on your radar.

For a faster, practical insulation solution, seal any of the bottom gaps under your garage door with rubber weatherstripping.

“If your budget and resources allow, however, the most effective way to retain heat in your garage is to insulate all the walls with fiberglass insulation,” says Chris Hunter, director of customer relations at ServiceTitan in Glendale, CA.

Regardless of your choice, these solutions will help decrease your energy bill and create a more comfortable environment.

Since the garage door is the largest opening in your home, investing in an insulated garage door may be worthwhile. Entry-level insulated doors typically provide an R-value between 6 and 9, while higher-end models can reach R-values of around 20.

“The higher the R-value, the higher the insulation capabilities and less heat loss that will occur,” explains Sharpe.

You don’t have to expose your valuables to the risks of an uninsulated garage.

“To avoid damaging your items in the garage during winter, you may either elevate them or bring them inside your insulated home,” says Tamer Sayed, licensed HVAC technician and the owner-operator of Tamas Mechanical in Mississauga, Ontario.

Before the winter begins (or even after, if you missed the boat), consult an HVAC professional for an insulation evaluation. The pro can determine whether your garage is properly safeguarded for the season and recommend the best next steps.

#5490. A Mortgage Rate Buydown Could Make Your Next Home More Affordable

You want to find the right home, but you also need the right monthly payment. And that can be hard when it feels like just about everything right now is putting a squeeze on your budget.

But there’s a tool that can help, and many buyers have never heard of it – it’s called a rate buydown. Here are the basics.

When you’re borrowing money to buy a home, it usually works like this. The higher your mortgage rate, the bigger your monthly payment. And with rates where they are now, some buyers are feeling the crunch. That’s where a buydown can really come in handy.

A buydown lets you pay some money upfront to get a lower mortgage rate – and by extension a better monthly payment. Basically, it’s a way to get a lower mortgage payment without waiting for mortgage rates to fall.

There are two main types, and they work a little differently.

A temporary buydown lowers your rate for a specific amount of time – usually the first one to three years. When the buydown period is up, you begin making the full payment amount. The loan’s official rate stays the same – you’re just getting help with part of the payment in the early years.

Think of it like a gift card for your mortgage. Money goes into an escrow account at closing. Each month, part of your payment comes out of that account instead of your pocket.

Here are the most common options when it comes to temporary buydowns:

1-0 buydown: Your rate is 1% lower for the first year.

2-1 buydown: Your rate is 2% lower the first year and 1% lower the second year.

3-2-1 buydown: Your rate is 3% lower the first year, 2% lower the second, and 1% lower the third.

A permanent buydown is a bit different. The big draw here is that they last for the entire loan, which could be 15 or 30 years – not just a couple of years like a temporary buydown. But normally, the monthly savings are smaller.

It’s paid for with points. Generally, one point equals 1% of your loan amount. And each point usually lowers your rate about a quarter of a percentage, but this differs from lender to lender. The important distinction?

A temporary buydown gives you short-term payment relief.

A permanent buydown can lower your payment for as long as you keep that mortgage.

With more homes available for sale, more sellers and builders are offering incentives to attract buyers. Some are even willing to pay for your buydown.

And whether that’s advertised up front or something you ask for in negotiations, it can have a bigger impact on your bottom line than you’d think.

Take a look at this example comparing a seller-funded 2-1 buydown with a permanent buydown on a median-priced home. In this scenario, the seller would pay for the upfront buydown costs. Remember, these are estimates – your numbers will vary:

In this example, the temporary buydown provides roughly $520 in monthly payment savings during the first year, compared with about $170 a month from a permanent buydown.

That’s a big difference in the short term. But there’s an important tradeoff.

As mentioned before, the temporary buydown savings don’t last forever. Once the buydown period ends, the full mortgage payment kicks in. That’s why it’s important to compare the numbers over time, not just during the first year.

This is where a lender can really help you explore your options. A buydown isn’t automatically the best choice for every buyer. It depends on your budget, how long you plan to stay in the home, and what you’re trying to accomplish.

A temporary buydown could give you extra room in your budget during the first couple of years, when you’re also managing moving expenses and settling into your new home. And if you expect your income to go up over time, this can be a good option.

On the flipside, a permanent buydown could make more sense if you plan to stay put for years and want the reassurance that the savings are sticking around until you move.

Either way, if you’re considering a buydown, the advice is simple.

Make sure you can comfortably afford the full mortgage payment, even if you’re starting with a temporary reduction.

Factor in what it could look like if the payment goes up after the buydown period ends. You want to be sure your budget can handle it.

Remember, lenders check whether you can afford the full payment, not just the discounted amount.

If you've found a home you love but the monthly payment is giving you pause, talk to your agent about buydowns. Then, meet with your lender to see the real numbers for your situation.A buydown could give you another way to make the numbers work, especially if a seller or builder is willing to help. Who knows it may just be the difference between  "maybe someday" and "welcome home."

#5489. Post-quantum cryptography startup Q.security launches with $11.5M in funding

Post-quantum cryptography startup Q Security Inc. formally launched today with $11.5 million in new funding for a platform designed to take enterprises from discovery through to completion of their quantum-safe migrations.

Founded this year, Q.security offers a remediation platform that runs the move to post-quantum cryptography as one coordinated program. The company argues that security teams need business context to decide which cryptographic findings to address first, since the time and resources available for the work are limited.

At the core of the Q.security offering is a map of an organization’s business structure and applications. Findings from the cryptographic inventory are tied back to that map, with the highest-risk assets put at the front of the queue.

Teams are said to be able to investigate exposure and work through remediation using a conversational artificial intelligence interface. Through integrations with existing cybersecurity and infrastructure tools, the platform drives fixes to completion using AI-guided runbooks, ticketing and automation.

Once a fix is in place, Q.security verifies that it works. Monitoring of the organization’s cryptographic posture then continues as standards and threats change, an approach the company claims lets security teams reduce risk faster and at lower cost.

“Quantum computing is making cryptographic risk an urgent and ongoing business priority,” said Guy Peer, co-founder and chief executive of Q.security, who previously co-founded Unbound Security and led its research and development through its acquisition by Coinbase Global Inc., announced in 2021.

Peer’s co-founder, Nir Steinherz, was director of product at Coinbase and vice president of strategy and product at Unbound Security. He was also a senior vice president at Citigroup Inc.’s Security Innovation Center, where he led secure digital banking initiatives for more than 100 million customers. The pair are said to have led a cryptographic migration protecting hundreds of billions of dollars in assets.

The funding is intended to support Q.security as it brings its platform to enterprise customers through direct sales and channel partners.

Castle Island Ventures led the seed round, with New York Life Ventures, Coinbase Ventures, Fin Capital, SBI US Gateway Fund and Ground Up Ventures also participating.

Matt Walsh, general partner at Castle Island Ventures, said enterprises know they need to prepare for the day quantum computers can break current encryption. With harvest-now, decrypt-later data collection already under way, “the challenge is determining how to prioritize the migration across business and technology environments,” he added.

#5488. Thinking About Taking Your House Off the Market? Read This First.

Between travel plans, family gatherings, and everything else this time of year can bring, selling your house may feel like just another squeeze on your calendar.

And if your house is already on the market, you may be wondering whether it’s worth keeping it listed. Maybe you’re even asking yourself: Wouldn’t it be easier to take a break and try again after the new year?

Before you decide, you should know there are some very real advantages that make staying on the market worthwhile.

Typically speaking, fewer people shop for homes toward the end of the year. And yes, that’s feeling even more true with rates where they are now. But here’s what you have to remember…

You don’t need dozens of people to fall in love with your house. You just need the right one. And the people who are still looking often have a pretty good reason they need to move.

Maybe they’ve accepted a new job that starts in early 2027.

Maybe their family needs more space and they’re trying to move during school breaks.

Or maybe something in their life has changed, and waiting until spring simply isn’t an option.

“Yes, things typically slow down in the weeks leading up to the holidays. But there are still people actively looking for homes and ready to pounce—or those who just entered the market on a short timeline and need to buy fast.”

The buyers looking now are exactly the types of buyers you want to see. They’re serious. They’re motivated. And they want to make this work.

Here’s another reason to think twice before taking your house off the market: other sellers may be having the exact same thought.

As the year winds down, fewer homeowners typically put their houses up for sale. And the latest data shows that’s happening again.

According to HousingWire Data, the number of new listings fell 13.4% from mid-October to mid-November 2026, and is down 7.1% year-over-year – the steepest annual decline since 2022. And that’s actually good for sellers who already have their homes listed for sale (see graph below):

For sellers who stay on the market, that means fewer of those fresh newly-listed houses to compete with. Sure, you may have other homeowners whose house has been listed for a while, but there won’t be nearly as many of those shiny, enticing “just listed” properties drawing your buyer’s attention away.

Keeping your house available gives it a chance to be seen while other homeowners are waiting for the calendar to turn. And that could mean more eyes on your house.

There’s also something to be said for keeping the momentum you’ve already built.

Your house is listed. The photos are done. Buyers can find it online. And your agent can continue marketing it to people who are actively looking.

If you take your house off the market, you could miss someone who’d be interested. But here’s the important part: staying on the market doesn’t mean you shouldn’t make adjustments.

If your house hasn’t attracted the offers you expected, this may be the perfect time to revisit your strategy.

Does the price still make sense compared to the competition?

Could better photos, staging, or a few small updates help your house stand out?

Would a price cut or upfront incentive be enough to get buyers interested?

Those are conversations worth having with your agent now, rather than assuming a new year will automatically bring a different result.

And you don’t have to put your life on hold for showings, either. Work with your agent to find a schedule that makes sense for you and your travel plans this season.

The end of the year may be busy for you, but that doesn't mean the housing market is closed for business. There are still motivated buyers looking and fewer new listings are coming onto the market.Before you decide to take your house off the market, talk to your agent about what’s happening locally and whether staying the course could help you get your house sold.

#5487. Buying a Home Soon? This Overlooked Open Enrollment Perk Could Save You Thousands in Legal Fees

Buying a home comes with enough expenses already. Between inspections, title insurance, closing costs, and a stack of paperwork that seems to grow every day, it's easy to lose track of what you're paying for.

But what if your employer could help cover some of the legal bills?

It's a possibility many homebuyers may overlook during open enrollment, when employees are typically comparing health insurance premiums and retirement benefits rather than thinking about hiring a lawyer.

Employer-sponsored legal plans, offered through companies such as LegalShield, MetLife and ARAG, can provide access to attorneys for a modest monthly fee.

A real estate attorney can review a purchase agreement, make sure inspection and financing contingencies actually protect the buyer, check the deed and title, examine mortgage documents, and represent a buyer at closing. Depending on the plan, some or all of that may be covered.

Jago Gavin, a LegalShield representative who works with employer groups, tells Realtor.com® that the real value is having someone to consult before signing something you might not fully understand.

"The law is not logical; it's legal," Gavin says.

That's relevant when buying a house, where an unfamiliar contract provision can have expensive consequences.

Gavin recalls a LegalShield member whose attorney spotted a potentially unfavorable mediation clause in real estate paperwork and recommended changing it before the buyer signed.

The potential savings can run from hundreds to thousands of dollars. But there's a catch: Not all legal plans offer the same services, and buyers need to know what they're getting before signing up.

Group legal plans work much like other voluntary workplace benefits. Employees pay a monthly premium, usually through payroll deductions, in exchange for access to specified legal services.

The price can be surprisingly affordable.

In a review of publicly available employee benefits documents, Realtor.com found a plan offered to employees of financial technology company Fiserv through MetLife for $15.50 monthly. LegalShield's published employer plans generally cost about $19 to $25 a month, depending on the coverage and employer.

That's roughly $186 to $300 annually, potentially less than the cost of a single consultation with a private attorney.

The plans typically provide access to participating law firms that handle matters ranging from contract reviews and consumer disputes to estate planning. Some cover specific services in full, while others offer discounted rates for legal work outside the plan.

ContractsCounsel, an online marketplace connecting clients with attorneys, reports that lawyers on its platform charged an average flat fee of $620 to review a real estate purchase agreement, based on completed projects.

Compare that with LegalShield's published Choice plan, which costs $21.95 monthly, or $263.40 over a year.

If an employee uses the plan for comparable document-review work without additional charges, the potential savings could be about $350.

But reviewing a contract and representing someone throughout a real estate transaction are two very different services.

LegalShield's published employer-plan documents include certain residential mortgage-document reviews but specifically exclude an attorney's attendance at closing. Documents must also be provided at least five business days before the scheduled closing.

An ARAG legal plan available to University of California employees, for example, pays participating attorneys for covered services that include reviewing and preparing home purchase documents and attending a closing. California doesn't generally require attorneys at residential closings, but the benefit illustrates how coverage can extend beyond reviewing paperwork.

The MetLife plan offered to Fiserv employees also lists home purchases and sales among its covered services. MetLife plan descriptions published by several other employers go further, listing deeds, boundary and title disputes, and property tax assessments—handy if a new owner wants to challenge a tax bill after the purchase. Employees should still check precisely what their particular plan includes.

And even comprehensive coverage won't eliminate ordinary closing expenses. Buyers are generally still responsible for title insurance, recording fees, taxes and other third-party charges.

New York real estate attorney Adam Leitman Bailey sees the obvious appeal: lower costs. But he questions whether attorneys with busy, established practices have much incentive to participate in programs requiring them to accept reduced fees.

For a relatively straightforward transaction, that might not matter much, he says. But complicated purchases can be another story.

"When something goes wrong, and this is the biggest investment of your lifetime, you'd better believe that you should be hiring the best attorney you can," Bailey tells Realtor.com.

That doesn't mean attorneys participating in group plans are necessarily less qualified. It does mean buyers should ask about their experience, particularly if a transaction involves title disputes, unusual contract provisions, or other complications.

Gavin acknowledges that LegalShield sometimes encounters coverage gaps in rural areas, where the nearest participating firm may be hours away.

Some plans offer referrals, discounted services, or reimbursement for using attorneys outside their networks, but those benefits vary.

Before relying on a workplace plan to handle a purchase, buyers should make sure an appropriate attorney is available and that the services they need are actually covered.

Buying a home is also a good time to think about what happens to the property in the future.

Many employer legal plans include estate planning services such as preparing wills and powers of attorney.

Some also help with living trusts, whether revocable, which can be changed later, or irrevocable, which generally can't. Either can help manage and transfer assets, and property properly placed in a trust can typically avoid probate.

These services can be expensive on their own. A March 2026 study by LegalTemplates, drawing on pricing from 909 law firms nationwide, found a median price of $625 for a standalone will and $2,475 for a revocable living trust.

By comparison, some employer legal plans include those services in the annual premium, potentially saving homeowners considerably more than they pay for coverage.

Becci Powers-Johnson, an eight-year LegalShield retail customer who became an independent associate selling its services in August 2026, says she and her fiancé have used the program several times to update their wills, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives.

"It was more than just the forms; it was the consultations that were included with it," she says. LegalShield offers unlimited consultations.

Of course, not every homeowner needs a trust, and some plans charge extra for preparing one or transferring property into it. The appropriate documents depend on individual circumstances and state law.

If you're thinking about buying a home in the coming year, take another look at your workplace benefits before open enrollment ends.

Start with your state's rules. Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Massachusetts, South Carolina, and West Virginia are among the states that require or customarily expect an attorney's involvement at closing, according to the National Notary Association, and in places like New York, it's standard practice. Elsewhere, a title or escrow company usually handles the closing, so full closing representation may matter more in some states than others.

Then check the plan itself. Does it cover purchase agreements, title and deed work, mortgage paperwork, or full closing representation? Is there an attorney near you who handles real estate transactions? And what happens if you need more complicated legal work?

Timing matters, too. You can typically sign up only when you're hired or during open enrollment, and many plans expect you to stay in for the full plan year.

George Washington University, for one, doesn't let employees cancel until the open enrollment after 12 months in the plan. Others allow cancellation at any time but make you wait until the next enrollment period to rejoin. And matters already underway may not qualify for coverage.

Even a relatively inexpensive plan isn't necessarily worthwhile if you never use it. But for someone preparing to purchase a home, the right benefit could pay for itself with just one covered legal service.

#5486. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul Signs New Private Listings Bill

New York has signed a new private listings bill, which means that properties will be required to be visible to the public as they hit the market unless the seller signs an informed opt-out consent.

Late last week, Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listing Act. The language of the bill requires that real estate listings be marketed in "at least one other publication, platform or website that does not require payment" or for the consumer to work with the brokerage for access.

This follows a quick path through the state's Legislature, which approved the act in a noncontroversial vote in June. The New York State Association of Realtors® strongly supports the bill.

This becomes the latest crackdown on private listings, where a real estate agent markets a property to a limited list of buyers before making it public.

Fair housing advocates say private listings raise discrimination concerns. One study from Bright MLS found private listings take longer to sell and don't guarantee more money.

The listing must be accessible to the general public, "without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise or select group of licenses." Also, there can't be restrictions on some or all of the details in the listing, according to the language of the bill.

The bill doesn't require a seller or lister to hold open houses or public showings if it violates any state or federal laws related to health and safety. And sellers can opt out, by signing a form that explicitly warns them that the listing will have limited visibility and possible impact on the price they get.

New York can punish violators with a fine of up to $5,000 and suspension or revocation of  their real estate license.

Earlier this year, the state saw its inventory of homes for sale fall to a 30-year low.

Washington and Connecticut have passed similar laws this year. Each has generally similar language in their bills, which also allow for opt-outs. A study from Zillow found the sales price of private listings was 1.3% less than comparable sales on the multiple listing service, costing the seller an average of $4,230 per sale. (Realtor.com® recently struck an agreement with Zillow to show preview listings from brokers who participate in Zillow’s preview program, in an effort to boost market transparency.)

Compass Inc., the real estate brokerage giant which has defended its use of private listings, said its recently unveiled See It First listings strategy complies with the law. It launched that program in September, which gives early access to homes that will soon be listed on the public market. Users don't need to work with a Compass agent to use it.

"New York’s new law preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes, including the ability to use a See It First strategy to test pricing and gauge demand," a Compass spokesperson said. "See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market."

New York has long struggled with housing affordability. The Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card gave the Empire State an F, the lowest rating possible. Hochul has emphasized affordability concerns and made a deregulation push to make home construction easier.

“My administration is focused on making New York more affordable and liveable for every New Yorker regardless of age or income, and housing is central to that goal,” Hochul said last week.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5485. Bootstrapped startup Levenza brings consumer-style personal agents to business workers

Artificial intelligence enthusiasts are embracing personal agents that can automate life’s most tedious digital chores, but office workers are still stuck juggling calendars, email messages and chat threads.

Levenza wants to change that with the launch of what it says are the first personal AI agents designed for corporate employees. The startup today announced the general availability of its enterprise-grade personal agents, together with its first acquisition in the shape of the AI research lab Fluid Inference.

In the last few months, personal AI agents have emerged as the hottest new trend in AI, sparking fierce competition among both technology giants and agentic startups. The biggest name is probably Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, a “secure by design” personal assistant that quickly shot to the top of U.S. app charts following its launch in September. We’ve also seen OpenAI’s Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, which aim to proactively get work done on behalf of their users, as well as startups such as Instinct, which raised a colossal $1 billion in funding in September for its consumer-focused agents.

AI agents may still be somewhat divisive, but the early success of Muse, Dots and Instinct shows that there’s clearly a large market for automated assistants. Yet those tools are all targeted primarily at consumers rather than enterprise workers, which means there’s a massive gap in the market that’s waiting to be filled. Levenza wants to be the one that fills it, with its personal agents developed specifically to run inside sensitive corporate environments.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Haefa Mansour (pictured, left) told SiliconANGLE that the difference between Levenza’s agents and those of its competitors is that it takes time to work with individual companies to customize what they can and can’t do. She explained that workplace agents can only provide value if they’re able to connect to corporate systems securely and respect a company’s dynamics and security policies.

“People have seen what personal AI agents can do outside of work, and they’re expecting the same experience inside the office,” Mansour said. “But most people at work are still spending hours every week coordinating schedules, cha50sing replies and tracking tasks. We built Levenza to take responsibility for that work.”

Levenza’s personal agents are designed to live inside of the platforms where work gets done, such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook and Slack. Within those environments, they act as proactive digital assistants for senior executives and other professionals.

Among other things, they can coordinate meetings across time zones, book hotel rooms, liaise with travel agencies, submit timesheets, triage overflowing email inboxes and send out replies and follow-ups when necessary. The more they do this work, the more they learn about the individual worker they’re serving, allowing them to become more useful over time, Mansour said.

By automating and coordinating routine work, Levenza’s agents can free workers from the “administrative drag” that affects every worker, slowing down productivity. “Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index found that the average worker receives 117 emails per day and is interrupted every two minutes,” Mansour said. “On top of the inbox and the calendar come the travel, expenses and follow-ups that slip through the cracks – none of this is work that professionals were actually hired to do.”

Mansour, a former Bain & Co. alumni who holds a Ph.D. from the University of California, founded Levenza alongside former Databricks Inc. and Uber Technologies Inc. engineer Austin Tackaberry (right) specifically to eliminate these distractions. The startup has made impressive traction, and despite not raising a dime in outside funding, its personal agents are already up and running at more than 300 enterprise customers, serving more than 10,000 professionals at those customers.

Early adopters such as Hg Capital and Oliver Wyman LLC report that their employees are saving up to three hours daily by offloading mundane admin to Levenza’s personal agents. They can also deal with any problems that occur during someone’s day. “For instance, if a manager’s customer workshop is running late and they’re likely to miss their flight, they don’t need to worry,” Mansour said. “Levenza will reach out to the travel management company to rebook according to their updated schedule.”

This means the manager in question will be able to focus on the workshop, safe in the knowledge that they’ll still be able to get to where they need to go after it does finish.

The acquisition of Fluid Inference is all about making Levenza’s agents more accessible. Mansour said the startup is an open-source research lab that’s focused on developing AI speech and ambient intelligence models.

By buying it, Levenza will be able to integrate natural voice interactions with its agents, so workers won’t have to tell them what needs to be done. Fluid Inference’s founder Brandon Weng is going to stick around as Levenza’s new head of engineering, adding much-needed talent to its team.

With Levenza’s agents now generally available, Mansour says the company will use its growing revenues to expand its third-party integrations and develop more capabilities for them. The company plans to launch automations for travel booking and expense management early next year, but that’s just the beginning.

“In the future, Levenza agents will operate with full autonomy in the enterprise, proactively deciding what work needs to be done,” she said. “They’ll coordinate with groups of other Levenza agents to collectively accomplish tasks.”

#5484. Number of Engaged Home Shoppers Dropped to New Low Last Quarter: Zillow

A house-shaped cutout on an hourglass symbolizing real estate timing, investment decisions, property value, and the urgency of housing market trends.

As mortgage rates rose significantly from July through September, leaving fewer serious shoppers competing for each home on the market, new research released by Zillow Monday shows the home-buying demand last quarter fell to the lowest level the mega-portal has tracked.

According to the report, the number of engaged home shoppers per listing—people who saved or shared a for-sale listing on Zillow, signaling real interest beyond casual browsing—fell to 3.5 nationally in the third quarter of 2026. That is down 4.8% from a year earlier and the lowest level since Zillow began tracking the metric in the second half of 2023. The pullback was widespread, with engagement down from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, although major Florida markets were an exception, the report stated.

“Mortgage rates are still keeping many buyers on the sidelines, and as inventory continues to build we are seeing less competition for each home for sale,” said Treh Manhertz, senior economic research scientist at Zillow. “The long-running inventory recovery means sales are poised to bounce back if mortgage rates finally move lower. But for now, the pressure is on for rentals while the for-sale market is on hold.”

Zillow says higher mortgage costs are the most likely driver of the drop in engaged home shoppers. Mortgage rates averaged 6.43% in Freddie Mac’s July 2 Primary Mortgage Market Survey, and rose to 7.28% by October 1—among the steepest three-month rate increases since the 1980s. That jump in rates is enough to increase the monthly mortgage payment on a $400,000 home by nearly $200, from $2,008 to $2,189 (assuming a 20% down payment). Typical mortgage costs rose year over year in August, September and October, ending a 10-month streak of annual declines.

The research shows more homes are sitting on the market as shoppers pull back, spreading home-buying demand across more listings. As of October, for-sale inventory has risen on an annual basis for 35 consecutive months, though it remains 14.4% below prepandemic norms. New listings have been a mixed bag, up on a year-over-year basis in just six of the past 12 months, suggesting the inventory buildup is more a result of homes staying on the market longer than a surge of new sellers.

Nearly every major metro saw home shoppers pull back Zillow’s research shows the pullback was widespread. Seattle saw the steepest drop in engaged shoppers per listing, down 17.1% from a year earlier. Washington, D.C. (-15.5%), Louisville (-14.3%), Salt Lake City (-13.7%) and Minneapolis (-13.4%) followed.

Only six large metros posted gains, and four of them are in Florida: Jacksonville (+12.2%), Miami (+8.7%), Tampa (+4.2%) and Orlando (+0.8%). San Francisco (+5.1%) and Birmingham (+0.9%) were the others.

Buffalo (6.7 engaged shoppers per listing), Hartford (6.2), Providence (6.1), San Francisco (6) and San Diego (5.2) had the most engagement last quarter. Despite its 8.7% year-over-year bounceback, Miami was one of the coolest markets with just 1.9 engaged shoppers per listing. Only Houston (1.6) had fewer.

Luxury engagement holds steady while starter-home interest slides The report shows luxury listings—homes among the top 5% most valuable in a given metro—typically drew 6.4 engaged shoppers last quarter, flat from a year earlier. Starter homes—homes in the 5th to 35th percentile of home values in a given metro—typically drew 2.9 engaged shoppers, down 8.2% year over year.

This reflects the “K-shaped” housing market that has emerged. Economic headwinds such as slower hiring and rising inflation are prompting many households to delay major financial commitments like a home purchase. Higher-income households are in a different position. Stock market gains have boosted buying power, while higher mortgage rates have little impact on those who can make an all-cash purchase.

Rental market is seeing spillover demand With for-sale demand waning, many would-be buyers appear to be turning to rentals instead, Zillow states. Nationally, rental demand is up 22.1% from a year earlier, according to Zillow’s October Rental Market Report. Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for apartments. The typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, about $360 less than the monthly cost of owning a single-family home with 20% down.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

That reading comes as sentiment across crypto has turned deeply pessimistic. For now, $0.90 is the level to watch. Holding it could give XRP the breathing room it needs to reclaim $1 and put November’s sell-off behind it.

#5482. Innovaccer expands Gravity Voice AI agents with SpaceXSI’s Grok Voice model

Healthcare artificial intelligence company Innovaccer Inc. today announced that it has expanded its Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice, the speech-to-speech model from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company SpaceXSI, formerly xAI.

The integration is aimed at the routine calls that make up much of a health system’s phone traffic, such as booking a visit, refilling a prescription or asking about a bill.

Grok Voice is a speech-to-speech model from SpaceXSI that is said to offer subsecond time to first audio, native tool use and the ability to reason while it speaks. According to Innovaccer, the model was trained on real phone audio with interruptions, corrections and background noise in it. More than 25 languages are supported. A business associate agreement is available for Grok Voice, which is Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act-eligible.

Coming into the expansion, Innovaccer’s voice business has grown quickly. Patient voice interactions on the platform have gone from roughly 250,000 to more than five million in the six months since the agents went live. Customers using them are said to be booking significantly more appointments, with referral intakes tripled and documentation time per case down 90%.

“Healthcare Voice AI is moving from answering questions to doing work,” co-founder and Chief Executive Abhinav Shashank said. With Grok Voice, he said, the company is extending where its agents work across the healthcare journey.

Innovaccer’s Agents of Care on Gravity approach is designed so that software handles the bulk of administrative calls, such as scheduling and refills. A human stays in the loop on clinical conversations.

Existing customers will get Grok Voice first through upgrades, along with new customer deployments. Innovaccer plans to use it in scheduling, referrals, prior authorizations, refill requests, chronic care check-ins and annual wellness visit outreach, among other tasks.

The integration is set to extend beyond voice over time. Innovaccer says it will bring Grok models to its healthcare data through the Grok API, with plans for SpaceXSI’s Grok Build coding agent and Grok Bot AI agent as well. Healthcare-specific training and evaluation are to follow once the voice integration is live.

The integration comes about six weeks after SpaceXSI released Grok Voice 3.0, the latest version of the model. At the time, SpaceXSI said Starlink uses Grok Voice to answer about 20,000 customer calls a day, with roughly 70% resolved without a human. The SpaceXSI name was adopted earlier in October, following SpaceX’s acquisition of xAI in February and a rename to SpaceXAI in July.

Innovaccer is a venture capital-backed company that has raised about $675 million to date, including a $275 million Series F round in January 2025. Notable customers include Orlando Health, Adventist HealthCare and Banner Health.

Gravity Voice AI agents with Grok Voice capabilities are available now.

#5481. Jennifer Garner Lights Up Her L.A. Home for Christmas Before the Thanksgiving Turkey Hits the Table

Jennifer Garner is getting a head start on Christmas at her Los Angeles home, where thousands of lights are already twinkling and monogrammed stockings hang above the fireplace.

The 54-year-old actress shared a look at her holiday decorations on Instagram, revealing that even her greenhouse got a festive touch with a wreath of its own.

Thanksgiving preparations were underway in the kitchen, where Garner gave the turkey a trial run ahead of the big day. Her dogs and cat were dressed for the occasion, too, in turkey costumes.

“We’re ready over here,” Garner wrote in the caption.

Garner has been known to love the holiday season, having previously opened up about her favorite memories during a Nov. 4 episode of the "Happy Hour With Ina Garten" podcast.

“My favorite Thanksgivings were when my kids were really little, I think it was right at the end of 'Alias,' and it was at a big house,” said Garner, who shares Violet, 20, Seraphina, 17, and Samuel, 14, with her ex-husband Ben Affleck.

“My kids were little, and Ben and I were there, and we all cooked. Bradley made the stuffing and Victor made ... I think Victor’s sister came. It was just our little 'Alias' family cooking together. It was so special," she added, referring to her co-stars Victor Garber, Ron Rifkin, and Bradley Cooper.

Despite separating in 2015 and divorcing in 2018, Garner and Affleck have continued to celebrate the holidays together.

Last year, a source told People that the couple spent the holidays together in Los Angeles.

“Jen makes it very special. She’s such a great chef. She loves having her whole family together, too. Ben’s always welcome at her house,” the source told the outlet.
